preamble: The diphthong [oi] becomes a plain back rounded vowel when the front offglide is lost and the nucleus is kept. Proto-Italic dative singular *-ōi (Old Latin Numasiōi on the Praeneste fibula) became Classical Latin -ō. Ancient Greek ωι (dative -ῳ) lost its offglide during the classical and Hellenistic periods, so that from about the 1st century BC it was pronounced like plain ω. In advanced Southern American English /ɔɪ/ loses its glide, above all before /l/, so that boils approaches balls. In each case the palatal glide disappears and the rounded nucleus survives.

examples.from: Old Latin Numasioi 'to Numerius' (Praeneste fibula, dative singular -ōi < PIE *-ōi)
examples.to: Classical Latin Numeriō, campō 'to the field'
examples.note: The second-declension dative singular *-ōi monophthongized to -ō.

examples.from: Attic τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ [-ɔːi] 'to the man', ᾠδῇ 'with a song' with long diphthong ωι
examples.to: Koine [-ɔː]: the iota no longer pronounced
examples.note: The long diphthongs ᾳ, ῃ, ῳ lost their offglide from the classical period onwards. From about the 1st century BC they were no longer distinguished from ᾱ, η, ω, and medieval scribes wrote the silent iota as a subscript.

examples.to: [bɔːlz], close to British or New York balls
examples.note: Part of the Back Upglide Shift: /ɔɪ/ loses its glide and becomes [ɔ], particularly before /l/.
Cajun English shows glide weakening in all gliding vowels, including /ɔɪ/.

sources: Allen, W. S. (1987). Vox Graeca: The Pronunciation of Classical Greek (3rd ed.). Cambridge University Press. https://www.cambridge.org/9780521335553
Labov, W., Ash, S. & Boberg, C. (2006). The Atlas of North American English. De Gruyter. https://doi.org/10.1515/9783110167467
